candidates.title: Toshiba’s five-in-one microwave is getting a $130 price cut before Thanksgiving
candidates.full_text:
Your phone replaced your camera, your iPod, your alarm clock, and your GPS, and honestly nobody filed a complaint. Now the same thing is happening on kitchen counters. The microwave, air fryer, and countertop convection oven used to be three separate boxes fighting over the same two outlets, and appliance makers are folding them into one. Toshiba’s OptiChef PRO MAX combines microwave, air fry, convection, broil, and a combination mode in a single 1.3-cubic-foot countertop unit. It even borrows a little phone DNA: a 2.4-inch color screen that displays menus instead of cryptic codes.

The trick is keeping five functions from feeling like five instruction manuals, and Toshiba gives that job to the color screen. Inside are a top-mounted fan and heating element for air frying, an inverter for continuous microwave power, and a humidity sensor intended to help food reheat evenly without drying out. Toshiba says the cavity fits a 13-inch pizza or a whole chicken, covering a fair amount of weeknight cooking and holiday prep. Its microwave lineage stretches back to 1959, when it completed Japan’s first microwave oven. Launched in April 2025, the PRO MAX sits at the top of the OptiChef family.

For decades, microwave keypads have spoken in riddles, with numbered presets and abbreviations that send you hunting for a manual you threw out in 2014. The OptiChef PRO MAX swaps those codes for a 2.4-inch color screen with plain-language menus, paired with an LED-backlit touch keypad for those midnight snack runs. Toshiba includes 25 preset auto menus and one-touch sensor reheat. The body is a wide, low silver box, 21.8 inches across and 12.8 inches tall (55.4 by 32.5 cm), with proportions closer to a countertop oven than a dorm-room microwave. Opening the door takes two moves: lift and hold a release trigger, then pull the handle.

Toshiba keeps every instruction on the front panel, right where your hands already are, so nobody has to dig out a phone mid-recipe. I like that bet, because appliances get used by whoever happens to be hungry, and that person rarely wants to unlock anything first. Each extra cooking mode is one more chance for someone to give up, jab the start button, and hope for the best. Plain-language menus shrink that risk, turning air fry or combi mode into an option you simply pick from a list. Readable menus could save everyone, grandparents included, another trip to the manual.

The microwave uses Toshiba’s Origin Inverter, which delivers continuous power rather than the on-off pulsing a conventional microwave uses at lower settings. The aim is to warm Tuesday’s leftover lasagna without turning the edges to lava while the center stays cold. The built-in humidity sensor monitors moisture during heating to help regulate reheating, while ChefDefrost varies power levels for more even thawing, handy when the chicken is still a brick at 5 p.m. Broil handles bubbly cheese tops and a final hit of color on a gratin.

ChefFry Plus handles air frying with a top-mounted fan and heating element, a layout also used in dedicated air fryer ovens. The fan circulates hot air around the food for crisping, while convection baking covers roasted vegetables, cookies, or a tray of potatoes on the side. Combi mode pairs microwave energy with convection heat, which Toshiba says helps dishes such as whole chicken and casseroles cook faster and more evenly. Running both methods together could be useful when dinner needs to hit the table by 6:30.

At 1.3 cubic feet (roughly 37 liters), the OptiChef PRO MAX sizes its cavity for family dinners and holiday sides. A 13.6-inch turntable sits inside, wide enough for that 13-inch pizza. The microwave delivers 1,100 watts of output from 1,250 watts of input and runs on a standard 120-volt outlet. Measure your counter before ordering, because the unit needs ventilation space above, beside, and behind it, plus room for the door to swing fully open. Toshiba’s manual lists the exact clearances, so check them against that tempting gap under your upper cabinets.

Toshiba links the design to its “Details Matter” philosophy and the Japanese idea of takumi, a craftsman’s attention to detail. candidates.title: Casio’s analog G-Shock GAC-2500 lands in India with a rolling date window
candidates.full_text:
A G-Shock with no screen at all still feels like a trick, and the GAC-2500 pulls it off with hands and a rolling date window. Four colors, one dial. India got it this week at ₹9,995, after Japan, the US and the UK.

That India price lands close to the $145 Casio charges in the US, so the watch stays in starter G-Shock money on both sides of the world. You get the full analog layout at that price, not a cut-down version with pieces missing.

Price: $145 in the US; ₹9,995 in India Where to buy: Buy on Amazon

The dial runs a two-eye layout, with a small seconds subdial at 9 o’clock and a three-cell window at 3 o’clock. Nothing glows or scrolls. Casio calls that window the Multi-Mission Date. It shows the date on normal days, then swaps to stopwatch minutes and setting details when you change modes.

The full auto-calendar runs to 2099 and handles month ends and leap years on its own, so the date stays right without any fiddling from you. It reads clean at a glance. Raised bar indexes and Neobrite-coated hands keep the dial readable in the dark.

Knocks move it, briefly. Casio mounts the hour and minute hands with magnetic force instead of pinning them straight onto a shaft, and that choice changes how the watch takes a hit.

After a hard impact the minute hand can shake or sit slightly off, then it settles back into the right spot within a few minutes. Casio calls the setup the Shock Release Hand. A hand-shift function also slides the hands aside when they cover the date window or the subdial.

The resin case measures 46.7 by 44.5 by 12.7 mm and weighs 47 grams, so it wears lighter than the numbers suggest on paper. Water resistance is 200 meters. You also get shock resistance, a 30-minute stopwatch, an amber LED light and mineral glass. The CR1025 battery lasts about two years, and a sleep mode parks the seconds hand to stretch that further.

The catch is the battery itself, since there’s no solar charging and no Bluetooth anywhere in this watch. You swap a coin cell every couple of years, and that’s the whole maintenance list, with no charger and no app in sight.

Price: GAC-2500 $145 in the US and ₹9,995 in India, in black, green, white and yellow Where to buy: Buy on Amazon

At $145 in the US and ₹9,995 in India, the GAC-2500 costs about what a nice dinner out runs, with a battery swap every two years as the only upkeep. This one’s for analog fans who want G-Shock toughness without a screen lighting up their wrist. Screens stay optional here. Gadgeteer covered the US launch earlier this month, and the India release closes the loop for buyers who watched that one from outside.

candidates.title: This Tiny Home Makes Room for a Proper Lounge in Just 20 Feet
candidates.full_text:
The Aria 20 gives its living room something easily lost in a tiny house: a clearly defined place to sit. Built by Georgia-based Dragon Tiny Homes, this 20-foot house on wheels places a dedicated lounge alongside a compact kitchen, with sleeping space overhead. The available inventory model lists 170 square feet downstairs, plus an approximately 91-square-foot loft. Its appeal lies in how deliberately those areas are divided.

Outside, two-tone engineered wood siding and a metal roof give the house a straightforward, residential character. It sits on a double-axle trailer, while the interior pairs shiplap walls with vinyl flooring. The lounge accommodates a sofa, with a television mounted nearby and a mini-split unit above. Large windows punctuate the living area, keeping the compact room visually connected to its surroundings.

The kitchen follows a galley arrangement, with a two-burner cooktop and a sink rather than an expansive cooking zone. This particular build adds a 7.1-cubic-foot stainless steel refrigerator, a range hood, upper cabinets, and a pantry cabinet. Those additions matter in a house where groceries and cookware need somewhere to go. A small dining and working nook provides a surface for one person, a useful inclusion with an obvious limit.

Storage continues into the staircase, which incorporates cupboards and shelving instead of leaving the space beneath the treads unused. It’s a sensible consolidation of two necessities: getting upstairs and putting things away. Dragon also includes shelving below the kitchen counter on this unit. Together, these choices assign storage to circulation and furniture zones rather than demanding another freestanding cabinet.

Upstairs, the loft has room for a king-size mattress, according to the builder. A built-in privacy wall gives the sleeping area some separation from the room below. This remains a low-ceilinged loft, though, rather than a bedroom with standing room. For anyone considering daily use, the question is less about mattress size than willingness to climb stairs every night and accept limited headroom at the top.

The bathroom occupies the opposite end from the lounge, fitting a shower, toilet, and sink into the compact plan. Dragon’s general Aria specification describes a sliding barn door, which avoids reserving floor space for a hinged door’s swing. The inventory listing also identifies provision for a combination laundry appliance, though buyers should confirm the included equipment.

Dragon currently lists this upgraded Aria 20 at $49,950, discounted from $55,695; the model’s advertised base price is $50,000. That distinction matters because the cabinets, refrigerator, television, and other additions belong to this inventory package. The most convincing part of the design is its allocation of space: a permanent bed upstairs leaves room downstairs for a sofa that doesn’t have to become one. The compromise is making that upstairs trip routine.
